articles.title: The Best GTA Missions
articles.summary: From wild heists and nostalgic drug deals to jetpack joyrides and beyond, these are the very best GTA missions of all time.
articles.body:
The five modern mainline GTA games (and by that, we mean from Grand Theft Auto 3 onwards) contain 346 story missions. 346 opportunities for blockbuster moments, unforgettable sandbox spectacles, career-making crimes, and the occasional excruciating nightmare. But among the missed trains, RC planes, and yoga sessions are some of the most memorable gaming experiences ever crafted, courtesy of developer Rockstar Games. These are the missions that propel us to that next letter on the minimap, the ones that start with a goofy cutscene and end with an orchestra of explosions and emotions.

These are the greatest Grand Theft Auto missions.

The first moments of Grand Theft Auto 3 are among the most impactful in gaming history. The scene is set in just five short minutes: an opening credit roll accompanied by jazzy piano, a bank heist and betrayal, and an armored convoy attacked on a dark and stormy night in Liberty City. After protagonist Claude is inadvertently freed from his prison transport, fellow escapee 8-Ball gives us our inaugural GTA mission, the first of many, many more to come.

Truth be told, “Give Me Liberty” is incredibly simple. Now trapped in Portland, you and 8-Ball simply drive to a safehouse, then drive to Luigi’s. There’s no real challenge, but as an onboarding experience it’s hard to overstate just how important a first mission can be. Similar titles of the era such as Driver and Stuntman were infamous for brutal tutorials that either bored the player to death or frustrated them to the point of quitting, and it’s not hard to imagine a world where GTA 3 forced you to do slaloms and handbrake turns in a parking garage before letting you loose in the sandbox.

“Give Me Liberty” isn’t just an introduction to a game, it's a bold statement of the series’ evolution and ambitions. In the top-down games, missions were more like goals than in-depth stories, conveyed exclusively through the medium of payphones with a few lines of unvoiced text. “Give Me Liberty” couldn’t be more different, with moody shots of the city establishing a cinematic atmosphere as hazy headlights smear through pouring rain punctuated by flashes of lightning. The vibes are, frankly, immaculate, especially when experienced on the original PS2 hardware, perfectly setting the tone for what GTA would become.

“Museum Piece,” like many GTA missions, begins with the protagonist being chewed out in a cutscene. After some heated words between Niko Bellic and mobster Ray Boccino, Niko agrees to sell $2 million worth of stolen diamonds in exchange for Ray’s help locating Niko’s former comrade-in-arms Florian Cravic. It’s a fairly standard pretext for some fun criminal action-adventure, but this one is special for two reasons:

The first is the setting. Unlike a typical back-alley exchange, “Museum Piece” takes place at, you guessed it, a museum. The Libertonian, to be precise, a hybrid of New York’s real-life Met and Museum of Natural History. Spoiler alert: the deal goes south, leaving Nico with no diamonds, no money, and legions of mobsters and cops out for his blood. The resulting shootout sees you blasting through the hallowed marble halls of a dimly lit museum after hours, shattering priceless artifacts and even destroying a dinosaur skeleton that took the developers so long to make they left a salty plaque behind as an easter egg. It’s one of the most unique interiors in the entire series and a refreshing change of pace from seedy warehouses and garages.

What really makes this mission special is that it’s a look into the future. Niko is accompanied on his mission by Johnny Klebitz, the player character from The Lost and the Damned DLC, and the mysterious sniper who breaks up the diamond deal turns out to be Luis Fernando Lopez, the protagonist of The Ballad of Gay Tony. All three stories converge on “Museum Piece,” and in their respective expansion packs we get to see how the deal goes down from Johnny and Luis’s point of view. One mission, three different perspectives. Sound familiar? Switching between characters would become a key part of the Grand Theft Auto formula beginning with 5, but “Museum Piece” pulled it off first.

If there’s one word to describe the missions in GTA: San Andreas, it’s “variety.” CJ’s wild journey from his mom’s old house on Grove Street to Mad Dogg’s mansion in Mulholland sees him racing go-karts, robbing houses, stealing farm equipment, waging war with remote-controlled toys, flying cross-country to Liberty City, and much, much more. There’s so much diversity and possibility within San Andreas that it can even incorporate completely different genres. Case in point: “Black Project,” in which CJ all but straps on a bandana for some Metal Gear-style tactical espionage action.

In a scene straight out of Ground Zeroes (which wouldn’t appear for another ten years,) CJ finds himself infiltrating a top-secret military base on behalf of the Truth, a zonked-out old hippie with a psychedelic van who does Tai Chi on the back of derelict airplanes. The Truth is one of the best quest-givers in the entire series, a hilarious throwback to the days before social media when conspiracy theories were the realm of harmless kooks instead of algorithms designed to destroy our shared concept of reality. He sends CJ to the fabled “Area 69,” where the government is keeping a classified black project under lock and key.

Solid CJ has several options. He can shoot out some searchlights to sneak past guards, or just snipe them from afar. He can open the base’s blast doors or crawl through a ventilation shaft to gain entry. Once inside, he has the option to disable the facility’s defenses to make his escape easier, or just run and gun with reckless abandon until he reaches the prize: an ultra-classified, state-of-the-art, $60 million jetpack. Carl Johnson soaring out of “Area 69” with rockets strapped to his back as soldiers try to shoot him out of the sky might be the peak of the series’ silliness, a glorious monument to the weird and wonderful wackiness of the “3D era” games. Frankly, it’s hard to top, which is why Rockstar might have dialed things way back with GTA 4.

An open world game like Grand Theft Auto has to do a lot of different things right at the same time: driving, shooting, swimming, dancing… it’s inevitable that something is going to suffer. Flying has never been GTA’s strong suit, from the clipped-wing Dodo of GTA 3 to the tedious “Flight School” and infuriating “Supply Lines” of San Andreas. You can’t even fly planes in GTA 4, and frankly, we didn’t miss it all that much. Flying would return in a big way with GTA 5, with one mission in particular finally delivering on the promise of vertical violence.

“Minor Turbulence” is a Trevor-only experience, the first mission after he and Michael are exiled from Los Santos. Trevor receives a tip from his long-suffering sycophant Ron that a Merryweather cargo plane full of military equipment is circling Mount Chiliad. Still salty over losing his ill-gotten gains from the last heist, Trevor takes to the skies in a dinged-up old cropduster to take down the massive jumbo jet.

We’d seen similar missions in previous games, but those all involved infiltrating from the ground. GTA 5 ups the intensity with a mid-air invasion that sees Trevor dodge rockets as he plows his biplane into the cargo hold of the much larger aircraft. After an awesome shootout dodging sliding 4x4s, Trevor takes over the cargo plane, only to be shot down by pursuing Air Force fighters, all to the tune of a god-tier Tangerine Dream track.

“Minor Turbulence” is a blockbuster mission that rivals the cinematic setpieces of Uncharted. More importantly, it’s fun. You’re not steering through rings or worrying about fuel or time limits, and while Trevor is forced to fly underneath the radar of the nearby military base, it’s a perfectly-judged injection of friction that makes the mission exciting instead of aggravating.

One of the hallmarks of a great Grand Theft Auto campaign is the sense of progression throughout the story. We usually start as penniless street crooks hiding out in dingy motels, rising through the underworld ranks to become a feared and powerful kingpin by the endgame. GTA expertly doles out perks and amenities as the protagonist gains status, perfectly fueling the power fantasy of rags-to-riches crime stories like “Scarface.”

Vice City’s biggest inspiration is in full effect during “Rub Out.” Ricardo Diaz, the big boss who kicks off the whole story by getting Lance Vance’s brother killed, lives in a huge mansion on Starfish Island that is the spitting image of Tony Montana’s humble home. And since Tommy Vercetti winds up working for the man he swore revenge on, you’ll be seeing it a lot. Diaz flaunts his wealth and power throughout the story, making it extra satisfying when you finally get the chance to take him down.

Vercetti and Vance wage a full frontal assault on Diaz’s fortress, fighting through hedge mages and pools in the huge interiors that pay homage to the climactic massacre of “Scarface.” Once Diaz is disposed of and the dust settles, the entire place is yours. The Vercetti Estate comes complete with a respawning armory, an Infernus, a helicopter, and a bunch of brand new gang members gassing you up. There would be flashier pads throughout later GTA games, but Vice City was the first that made you feel like you’d finally made it.

6. “Breaking the Bank at Caligula’s” - GTA: San Andreas

The top of this list is going to be heist heavy, and for good reason. A great heist is the essence of all that is GTA: big brazen crimes, outrageous objectives, and open-ended improvisation when things go wrong. There had been heists in Grand Theft Auto before “Breaking the Bank at Caligula’s” – Vice City had a similar quest chain to rob the Corrupto Grande bank – but this was the first one that felt truly huge . San Andreas released just three years after Ocean’s Eleven ushered in the modern era of heist films, and the game aimed high with a similarly spectacular casino job that set the bar for future generations.

After Woozy makes CJ a full partner in the Four Dragons Casino, they decide to take out their biggest rival, Caligula’s, by robbing it blind. Setting up the job requires a variety of diverse objectives before things get underway – all of which CJ has to handle by himself. He has to woo and date a Caligula’s employee in order to obtain her keycard in exchange for a cut of the profits, steal four police motorcycles and an armored car, sneak into a city municipal building to snap some photos of the casino’s blueprints, and sabotage a giant dam to cut the power. It’s a lot of work, but in true San Andreas fashion every preparation mission feels unique and fun in its own way.

When it’s time for the heist itself, CJ dons a Caligula’s croupier outfit and infiltrates the casino with some mild, Hitman-esque social stealth. Once he’s in, CJ has to force open a garage door with a forklift, navigate the mazelike interiors with night vision goggles, lead a team of surprisingly cheerful accomplices to the vault, fight his way up to the roof and escape via parachute to a neighboring building in a stunt that would make Tom Cruise giddy, all within a heart-pounding seven-minute timer. “Breaking the Bank at Caligula’s” isn’t quite as impactful or in-depth as some future heists we’ll see on this list, but it remains an extremely fun and impressive feat for its time.

If you’re coming to GTA looking for branching narratives and tough story choices, you’re cluckin’ up the wrong bell. That’s not to say your choices have no impact on the plot, but they’re largely superficial: The smart way or the loud way; sparing your target or killing them; hiring the least expensive and most expendable goons for the heist or paying up for talented pros. “A Dish Served Cold” is a major exception.

In the final stretch of GTA 4, Niko Bellic is ordered by Jimmy Pegorino to conduct one last drug deal with the architect of his pain, Dmitry Rascalov, the mob boss who torments Niko throughout the game. Niko can take the deal at the behest of cousin Roman, begging him to leave revenge and bloodshed behind and start a new life. Or, if the pull of vengeance is too strong (and you don’t need the $250 grand), you can blow the deal and claim your retribution. The latter (and probably canonical) choice leads you to “A Dish Served Cold,” in which Niko wages an intense assault on Rascalov’s cargo ship and puts an end to their beef permanently.

It’s a fine mission, but it’s the repercussions that matter. If you ignore your inner demons and make the deal, Rascolov assassinates Roman on his wedding day. If you give in to your anger, Kate McReary – sister of Packie and a potential romantic interest who desperately seeks to escape the cycle of crime and violence – is killed in the crossfire of a Pegorino drive-by. They’re downer endings either way, gut-punching tragedies that reward you with a cheerful “You Won!” achievement amidst the anguish. “A Dish Served Cold” might be the most we’ve ever cared about GTA. It’s an unexpected, bittersweet resolution to the most human story the series has ever told, and it’s stayed with us ever since.

Not every GTA mission can be a thrilling, epic, crime adventure. Sometimes, especially when a campaign is just getting started, they’re about getting to know the characters better, exploring a location, and just existing in the world while doing crimes and making a little money. Few missions capture this “hangout” vibe better than GTA 5’s “Hood Safari.”

Shortly after the game unlocks all three playable protagonists, Trevor barges in on Franklin as he is having doubts about his future with the Chamberlain Gangster Families. Eager to get to know his new pal better, Trevor insists on accompanying Franklin, Lamar, and Chop on a drug exchange with the rival Ballas that takes them back to extremely familiar territory. Returning to the iconic Grove Street cul de sac a few in-game decades after Carl Johnson’s journey began in San Andreas is a masterful callback, not as intense as the visit to Shadow Moses in Metal Gear Solid 4, but a lot funnier.

GTA’s humor can be extremely hit or miss, but the combination of personalities and always excellent performances help “Hood Safari” nail the perfect balance between characterization and absurdity. Trevor is his usual unsettling self, but his experience comes in handy during the drywall handoff. Lamar is hungry to climb the food chain and get serious about his career, but he can’t help fawning over rapper MC Clip’s fashion shoot – even while stealing his jetskis. There’s plenty of action, with a good old fashioned Grove Street turf war and a great chase through the Terminator 2 canal, but the real treasures of this mission are the friends we made along the way.

Unlike other signature GTA heists, there’s no preparation involved in “Three Leaf Clover,” no tailing NPCs for intel or stealing a getaway car in advance, just a text from Packie McReary telling Niko to put on a nice suit for a big job. The gang takes over the Bank of Liberty in China town, but the mission goes south when a hostage who clearly peaked in high school takes out one of the crew while the others are busy blowing the vault.

A massive police response swarms on the bank as you battle your way out through the streets of Algonquin with a million dollars worth of cash stuffed in your duffelbags. It’s a mad dash as Niko and what’s left of his squad use abandoned cars for cover, scrambling through subway stations as they barely escape Homeland Security organisation NOOSE. If you can make it back to Dukes alive, you’re rewarded with access to Algonquin and $250,000, a huge sum of money for that point in the story.

If “Caligula’s” was Ocean’s Eleven, “Three Leaf Clover” takes its obvious cues from Michael Mann’s intense 1995 thriller Heat, with a tip of the hat to Point Break. The mission is clearly inspired by Heat’s immortal downtown shootout, so realistic that actual armed forces have used it as an example of urban combat skills. While it’s unlikely GTA 4 will ever be taught at West Point, it’s a perfect fit for the game’s gritty vibe. This isn’t some slick heist with disguises and stolen keycards – we’re in the world of balaclavas and plastic explosives. “Three Leaf Clover” is brutal, inelegant, and ugly – everything that makes GTA 4 unique among the series. Heck, it’s so good that characters are still talking about it in the sequel.

By GTA 5, heists had evolved into a central pillar of the campaign. There are six heists through the single-player story, each of which requires careful planning and prepping. Now systematized, heists are almost a game mechanic unto themselves, with a whiteboard planning phase that asks you to weigh risks and make decisions before the mission is a go. Who will you hire? Will you go loud or soft? Which spooky mask will you buy for your crew? Important questions, all, with unique consequences for each choice – though it’s hard to get too chuffed about your cut of the money when most of it ends up going to FIB anyway.

Most of the heists in GTA 5 are fantastic, and nearly any one of them could fill this spot on the list without much argument. “Blitz Play,” another Heat homage, sees you hijacking an armored car in broad daylight. Michael and Trevor’s dream job of robbing the Union Depository is a suitably epic climax, and “The Merryweather Heist” puts you in the frankly implausible position of controlling a high-tech deep-sea submersible with only a video game controller. Great missions, all, but when it comes to pure power fantasy, it’s tough to beat “The Paleto Score.”

Unlike most heists in GTA 5, you don’t have much of a choice when it comes to robbing the tiny rural bank in Paleto Bay. There’s no way around the alarm system, and the short police response time means there’s no chance of escaping under the radar, meaning it’s time to bust out the big guns. It begins a lot like the “Three Leaf Clover” heist, with Michael, Trevor, and guest barging into the lobby and taking hostages. While GTA 4 keeps things relatively grounded with its frantic footchase, The Paleto Score turns the tables and gives you the upper hand for a change.

As the local police surround the bank building, your crew emerges through the double doors decked out in heavy duty bomb squad armor and loading for bear. Wielding a minigun nicked from a military convoy, you blast through an army of country bumpkin cops and wreak havoc on the sleepy mountain town. The mundane scenery makes for an excellent explosive set piece as you shoot down helicopters and blow up cop cars while you wait for Franklin to gradually arrive with a getaway bulldozer. After dodging tank shells and a brief detour through a chicken factory, the gang catches a train and counts their earnings, just before Agent Sanchez shows up to snatch it all away.

“The Paleto Score” is the perfect middle ground between the cartoon craziness of “Caligula’s” and the grim verisimilitude of “Three Leaf Clover,” a brilliant example of the balancing act that defines modern Rockstar.

GTA campaigns can be long. Between all the cutscenes, travel, and quest-givers who just love stringing you along with tedious busywork, by the end of any given game you’re usually more than ready to roll credits. That’s why it’s so crucial for GTA to stick the landing and deliver excellent finales , which the series delivers more often than not. The big heist, the ultimate revenge, the culmination of hours and hours spent grinding your way up the criminal food chain – a great final mission doesn’t leave you spent and ready to move on to the next game, it revitalizes you and hypes you up to free roam throughout the postgame in the city you now rule. There have been some excellent final missions throughout the franchise, but they’ve never reached the same heights as “End of the Line.”

San Andreas is on fire. Literally. The entire city is shaken by the acquittal of Officer Tenpenny, the cop who's been using and tormenting CJ throughout the game. The chaos canonizes the infamous “pedestrian riot” cheats from the previous games as angry NPCs attack each other and cars explode in the distance. The altered world state makes End of the Line feel truly climactic – there’s no going back from this, and whatever happens, CJ, Los Santos, and all of San Andreas will never be the same again.

CJ and Sweet decide the time is finally right to take down the treacherous Big Smoke and his Ballas empire once and for all. After making their way to his fortress in East Los Santos, CJ commandeers a SWAT tank and smashes through the front door. He battles through three floors of Ballas, Vagos, Rifa, and Russian mobsters before barging in on Big Smoke, who is busy playing video games and hitting a bong. CJ takes him down, only for Tenpenny to spoil the moment, forcing CJ to shoot way back down the burning building and chase after the crooked cop, who is fleeing in a massive fire truck with Sweet dangling from the ladder.

Bombastic, brutal, and big in every sense of the word, “End of the Line” is the ultimate catharsis after 45 hours of grinding your way up from Grove Street. In clearing a huge game like GTA: SA, you share in CJ’s sense of accomplishment and closure when Smoke and Tenpenny take their last breaths. And as the group gathers to celebrate and discuss their plans for the future, CJ steps out into the hot Los Santos night alone, eager to “hit the block and see what’s happening.” The mission might be the “end of the line” for the San Andreas story, but for Carl Johnson, and us, the whole world is now our oyster and the journey is just getting started. It’s one of the best last levels of all time and, in our estimation, the greatest GTA mission ever.

What do you think of our GTA mission rankings? Did we leave out your favorite? Should we have shown Caida Libre more love? Did anyone out there have no problem following the damn train? Leave a comment to let us know, or vote in the poll above.

articles.title: The Steam Machine Is Better for Me Than the PS5 or Xbox Series X
articles.summary: The Steam Machine has been around for a month now, and it has perfectly settled into my daily gaming habits. Now, I can't imagine life without it.
articles.body:
The Steam Machine has been out for a little over a month, and while I spent the first couple of weeks testing it against the PS5 and different graphics cards, I wasn’t sure how or even if it’d fit into my daily rotation. But then this last weekend I came down with a cold, and I fell back in love with this little computer. Plugging it into my TV while laying on the couch, turning off the meters and just playing my Steam library? Let’s just say I see the vision.

I still don’t think it’s necessarily worth the high price for everyone, especially if you don’t already have a robust PC gaming library, but now, all I ever want out of this thing is to pick up whatever PC game I’m playing at my desk, and run it on the TV without tying up my network. And at that, I can’t really think of anything that does it as well as the Steam Machine, especially without taking up way too much space on my entertainment center.

I’ve never really been much of a console gamer. I still bought the consoles every generation, because I just think gaming hardware is neat. But whenever I buy a game, I usually just buy it on Steam, and it’s been that way for almost 20 years. The consoles just kind of filled in the gaps. Most of my library on either the PlayStation 5 or the Xbox Series X is made up of a few exclusives and a bunch of games that came with various subscriptions.

But even when I do buy exclusives for the PS5 or Xbox I don't really even play them. Just looking back to last year with Death Stranding 2 , I only got an hour or so in because the only way to play it was in my living room. So, I eventually forgot about it and moved on to the new thing.

PC is an entirely different story. Because I can pick up whatever I’m playing on whichever device I’m using, it’s way more likely that I’m going to finish any game I buy on PC. I spend most of my time playing at my desk, but it just so happens that I primarily play RPGs that have a lot of side quests or grinding involved. I love shutting the game down at my desk, then lying in bed playing through some of the content on a handheld while watching a TV show or listening to a podcast.

Even before I started reviewing hardware professionally I always had multiple PCs. I'm just built different I guess. One of the magical things about buying games on any of the PC platforms is that I can progress through them on whichever device I'm using at the time. A handheld, a laptop, my tower? All of which are great in different situations and they all play the same games with the same save data.

But the living room has always been an outlier for me.

I've had living room PCs in the past, but I've always been frustrated with the need to have a keyboard and mouse stashed away just in case I had to fiddle with something. That's not to mention how much a full tower PC stands out among the much more sleek consoles. Before the Steam Machine came out, I just kind of stopped playing games on the TV at all.

It just so happens that SteamOS almost entirely negates this problem. Pretty much all of the daily maintenance for the Steam Machine can be done in ‘Gaming Mode,’ without ever needing to go to the desktop. And, even when I do need to use the desktop, like when I’m getting third party launchers or games, the Steam Controller’s trackpads make it so that I don’t have to break out a keyboard and mouse.

Over this last weekend, the Steam Machine just kind of fell into its natural place. I set the outgoing resolution to 1440p, rather than 4K, and at the distance that the couch is from the TV, it looks just fine . Would it stand up if I zoomed in and started pixel peeping? Probably not, but the whole point of living room gaming is not doing that. And, so I spent the weekend playing Resident Evil 4 Remake and Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth in a Nyquil-induced haze, and it was incredible.

I honestly couldn’t tell you whether or not I was getting a steady 60 fps or not, or whether it looked better than the PS5. But it didn’t really matter. I got to carry on my saves from my PC and didn’t have to buy another copy of either of the games just to play them on the PS5 Pro that’s now collecting dust next to the Steam Machine.

At $1,049, the price-to-performance ratio is still bad enough to stop me from recommending the Steam Machine to anyone that just wants to play console games. But I own thousands of games on Steam, many of which don’t even exist on the PS5 or Xbox Series X. If you’re anything like me, just having a living room box that can play your entire Steam library locally, especially when it takes up half the space of other consoles, is a dream come true.

Jackie Thomas is the Hardware and Buying Guides Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

articles.title: GTA 5 Actor Auditioned for 60 Roles in GTA 6, But Heard Nothing from Rockstar
articles.summary: Actor Robert Bogue, who played FIB agent Steve Haines in Grand Theft Auto 5, says he auditioned for 60 roles in GTA 6, but he was ultimately ignored by Rockstar Games.
articles.body:
Actor Robert Bogue, who played FIB agent Steve Haines in Grand Theft Auto 5, says he auditioned for 60 roles in GTA 6, but was ultimately ignored by Rockstar Games.

The news comes courtesy of X user Burak , who DMed Bogue with some questions on Instagram. Despite the absurd secrecy revolving around Rockstar and GTA 6, Bogue was pretty forthcoming. The actor was asked whether or not he was involved GTA 6, to which he revealed that he's not, much to his dismay.

"I'm a little bit down on Rockstar right now," said the actor. "I had such a great time working with them. [...] I so badly wanted to work on GTA 6. I must've auditioned for over 60 characters. Some were big, some were small. I didn't care. I just wanted to be in it. I didn't get any of them, and they never called me about any of them. I was so disappointed. I thought maybe they have an unofficial policy where they don't reuse actors, because I thought, 'You're gonna say no to me 60 times? Even for a small character?' So, I'm a little furstrated by them. I feel like someone who's in love with a girl and then she just dumped me."

Bogue went on to state that he doesn't know anything about the game beyond what's publicly out there. Once these comments surfaced, Bouge relayed another message through Burak.

"I'm sorry to throw Rockstar under the bus publicly about how many auditions I've had, but the truth is the truth. At the end of the day, the actor's life is about rejection. It's just, sometimes you need a victory once in a while."

Bogue has worked with Rockstar more than once. He was Red Harlow in Red Dead Revolver, Troy in Grand Theft Auto: The Ballad of Gay Tony, and, as already noted, Steve Haines in Grand Theft Auto 5. It seems like Rockstar is definitely open to bringing back actors in other roles if it makes sense. Ned Luke, who played Michael in GTA 5, did a small role in Red Dead Redemption 2, but claims Rockstar removed his lines to avoid distracting players. It's possible Rockstar felt that Bogue would stick out in GTA 6 or simply believed he wasn't the right fit for any parts.

Nevertheless, Bogue's frustrations seem to mainly stem from the fact he was ghosted and never officially given an official rejection. Whatever the case may be, it certainly seems safe to say we won't see Steve Haines running around in GTA 6. That may not come as a total surprise, though, as players kill him in one of the game's multiple endings, and that ending is widely believed to be the canon one.

Bogue's frustrations are also not totally unique. Prior to GTA 5, Rockstar had several fallouts with actors, including Niko Bellic actor Michael Hollick. The actor told press that he felt he was underpaid, as he was only paid $100,000 for 15 months of work on GTA 4. When GTA 4 came out and was a massive commercial hit, Hollick felt frustrated that he didn't see a penny of that. It's believed that this dispute is why Niko didn't get a cameo in GTA 5, while characters like Packie, Michelle/Karen, and Brucie did.

Ray Liotta also made comments about the pay on Grand Theft Auto: Vice City being subpar compared to the films he was used to. Over time, the relationship between Rockstar and actors appeared to become better, with people like Roger Clark, Ned Luke, and Shawn Fonteno having nothing but nice words about their experience. Fonteno has noted that Rockstar has been kind to him, even if he's not entitled to any residuals. Both him and Luke have reprised their GTA 5 roles in updates for GTA Online, providing them additional work in a franchise they love.

Cade Onder is a freelancer for IGN's news team. He covers all things entertainment, including gaming, film, and more. You can find him on Twitter @Cade_Onder.

articles.title: The Original Pokémon Series Is Now Streaming on Disney+ — So Where Are All of the Episodes?
articles.summary: The original Pokémon TV series is officially streaming on Disney+. Some of it, at least.
articles.body:
The original Pokémon TV series is officially streaming on Disney+ . Some of it, at least.

Of the 80ish total episodes that comprise the original Indigo League arc , only 27 are now available on Disney+. That's not an entirely random number — the first season of Pokémon was split into three parts when it was brought to DVD in North America, and Disney's episode count lines up with what was included on Viz Media’s first compilation.

Netflix, which has long been the streaming home for most of the Pokémon series , continues to have the first 52 episodes. That number matches how the series was originally split up for annual North American broadcast schedules.

Unlike Netflix, which goes with the specific "Indigo League" title, the episodes on Disney+ can be found under the arc's broader title, “Pokémon the Series: The Beginning.” Both streaming services skip over the original 18th episode, “ Beauty and the Beach ,” which only aired a few times in the U.S. after some heavy editing.

You're not entirely out of luck if you're looking for the full 80-episode arc. Those last 26 episodes are available to stream for free with ads on YouTube and Tubi , and are also included in Warner Home Video's revamped DVD release from 2014.

Disney+ was already streaming most of the more recent Sun & Moon seasons as well as a small selection of Pokémon movies, including The Rise of Darkrai and Zoroark: Master of Illusions . The addition of the original arc marks the streamer’s first major move with the franchise since acquiring the streaming license earlier this year.

Disney also picked up the broadcast rights for the original series, meaning Pokémon is officially back on Disney XD schedules .

The Pokémon TV series has become pretty closely associated with Netflix, with the streamer even producing its own original series with the franchise, Pokémon Concierge . It’s not entirely clear what else Disney plans to do with its newly acquired streaming and broadcast rights, and whether we’ll ever get the full Indigo League arc (let alone the full series) on either streaming platform.

Pokémon as a whole is currently celebrating its 30th anniversary, which has naturally been a ripe occasion for announcements across all of the franchise's iterations. We're talking new TCG releases , plenty of Pokémon Go events , and even some LEGO sets .

Somewhat ironically, the mainline Pokemon games are actually skipping 2026, but we did get our hands on what I consider one of the best cozy games of the modern generation, Pokémon Pokopia . We also got our first look at Gen 10 , Winds and Waves, which included a glimpse at the three new starters .

Disney+ continues to chug along in its own right, though it no longer openly reports the number of subscribers across its particularly large number of plans and bundles . The company has recently been focused on diversifying what it offers through the Disney+ app, having just inked a deal with TikTok to bring user-made shorts to the service. The possibility of a free, ad-supported streaming option was mentioned during the company's most recent earnings call , but in the era of endless price hikes , I wouldn’t get too optimistic.

Blythe (she/her) is an Audience Development Coordinator at IGN who, when she isn't following streaming news, spends way too much time in character customization screens and tracking down collectibles.

articles.title: GTA 5’s Trevor Flipped the Bird at Rockstar's Haters
articles.summary: The Genius of Grand Theft Auto 5’s Trevor Philips: how Rockstar turned franchise backlash into an iconic character.
articles.body:
Ever since GTA 3’s protagonist (a stoic murder proxy allegedly named Claude) melted our hearts, every one of Rockstar’s rich and varied litany of leading men has reached iconic status. But there’s one that stands out as their most brilliant, subversive best.

Rockstar’s biggest triumph, though, is that their other greatest character isn’t subversive at all. In fact, he is Mr. GTA , absolutely everything you and your mum might associate with the series embodied in one gloriously nasty psychopath.

Trevor was created in part to solve the conundrum of what media wanks in the late '00s liked to call "Ludonarrative Dissonance", a phenomenon in games like this where the actions of the player in the open world are at odds with the motivations of the character.

It’s something that reached its most absurd extent in GTA 4, where you had a character whose Tinder profile would read “Sad About War” waging his own endless conflict against the LCPD, pigeons, bystanders, hot dog vendors, and anyone else. Depending on who was at the controls, of course. Essentially there are two Niko Bellics , two CJs , two Arthur Morgans : the character given voice by writers, and the avatar that exists only as a conduit for player agency. Usually to commit atrocities in the name of escapism.

GTA 5’s Trevor Philips is well understood to represent that sort of player. But he isn’t just a conduit, he almost is The Player made manifest in that universe. An ambassador for the user. A composite of playing styles given personality and an overactive sex drive, designed to evoke the way your wee brother plays GTA: that is, causing mayhem for the sake of it and achieving very little in the process. And imagining what happens when that specific GTA guy is given narrative agency.

His infamous introduction is as freeing as it is shocking: he enters the story of GTA 5 at perhaps his most vile. Motivated only by base desires. Brutally murdering a beloved former protagonist for merely speaking out of turn. At this point, GTA fans had spent dozens of hours playing as Johnny Klebitz in The Lost and Damned, a harrowing story of gangland betrayal that ends on a hopeful note, with Johnny cutting ties with the bad influences in his life and pledging to go straight. By the time we meet him again in GTA 5, he’s a sickly looking meth addict who has fallen right back into the world he’d managed to escape from.

But we barely got any time to think about that, because after swiftly kicking him to death, we as Trevor Philips had work to get on with. It’s a bold move to bring in a new character by diminishing an established one. It certainly can work, but it usually means the incoming character starts with an uphill battle to get the audience on their side.

You’d be forgiven for thinking that Trevor isn’t supposed to be liked at all. Some readings of GTA 5 call him the true villain of the piece: and it’s not hard to see why. On paper there’s nothing especially likeable about him. He doesn’t stand for anything, is a hateful jerk, and as an idea he’s about as complex as the wee ship in Asteroids. The challenge, then, is how to make such a character compelling without betraying the deliberate lack of complexity at his core. Surely nothing would ruin Trevor more than that wretched cowardly device we call nuance. I know writers who use subtext, etc. Everything Trevor does has to be in service of his immediate wants or his personal enrichment.

But complexity doesn’t have to mean riddled with contradictions. Trevor has a moral code of sorts, he values loyalty, not just to himself but as a general virtue, which is what fuels his deep-seated rage at Michael during his first story act. But, despite this delineating betrayal, he displays an unwavering allegiance to Michael’s young family, caring for his children to whom he considers himself an uncle.

As his fraught backstory becomes fleshed out in drips and drabs over the course of the game, the writers are keen to give any tragic revelations some ballast so they don’t ever become excuses or justifications for his behaviour. On the one hand, we find out that he has a history of childhood abuse and abandonment. On the other, it’s heavily implied that he’s an infamous serial strangler and a cannibal. We know that he’s a gifted aviator, but that his career as a fighter pilot is cut short in the eighties when he fails a psyche evaluation. It’s sort of hard to take Trevor’s side over the Canadian military in that instance.

Canadian. Yes, no doubt inspired by his actor Steven Ogg hailing from up north, Trevor who is about as antithetical from the concept of politeness as any human being can be, is from Canada. That Trevor is one of the core American archetypes – a troubled forces veteran who has been utterly failed by the system – and yet isn’t even American might be one of the best jokes in the entire game.

The player is rarely asked to feel sorry for Trevor. Even at his lowest ebb, where we see him briefly start to build a relationship with his estranged mother only for her to abandon him again, triggering a regressive outburst of psychological anguish, we’re forcibly transferred to a different character while the consequences of that are played out off-screen.

The great parlour trick that Rockstar pulls off with Trevor is to give him dimensions and layers enough to rival that of Niko Bellic, but without falling into the same trap of Ludonarrative Dissonance. In fact, it achieves a state of ludonarrative harmony : one not seen since Vice City avoided all this nonsense by having you play as a coke fiend. But unlike Tommy Vercetti’s inspiration Scarface, Rockstar becomes truly untouchable in the process: creatively and morally untethered, exiting the media’s field of influence on a rocket ship powered by cash.

By building a character who unapologetically embodies all the degeneracy that GTA used to be stereotyped with, Rockstar made a big joke at the expense of all their critics. By imbuing him with such brilliant, emotive depth, they garnished that joke with a raised middle digit.

The character was conceived at a time when Grand Theft Auto had a deep and seemingly unshiftable reputation in mainstream circles for being a mindless crime simulator, one that has no artistic merit, and merely exists to reward and glorify depravity and atrocity. Obviously, as gamers who enjoy Rockstar’s worlds and characters we know that assessment is, at best, reductive. But only with the passage of time and the changing of the guard when it comes to what and who “the media” reflects and represents, e.g. millennials, has this reputation been buffed away.

I suspect, if you didn’t live through it, it’s difficult to appreciate just how ingrained this dismissive, derisive attitude was. And let’s be honest, the original GTA didn’t exactly make the most intellectual first impression, with its simplistic objectives, crude visual design, and literal bonus points for massacring Hare Krishnas.

And, yes, look, though I would call it borderline cartoonish, ultraviolence is a core part of GTA’s design. There’s no getting around it. The freedom to be an unapologetic criminal, to reject and frustrate societal norms with outlandish behaviour, without any significant consequences, is integral to the appeal of a Rockstar Game. Because they’re rad.

Still, all the fan favourite Rockstar guys have a layer of complexity that makes them relatable, and endears them to us despite their capacity for depravity. Whether it’s that they’re sad about war, missing mom, or dying of tuberculosis, Rockstar is with each successive game imbuing its characters with ever more humanity and, in turn, more reason to get invested in the parts of its world that aren’t just a playground. We can certainly see this in the brewing love story that is GTA 6: I will die on the hill that says depicting real, quiet moments of tenderness between its lead characters is perhaps the studio’s grandest evolution to date.

Because it’s about people . There’s no such thing as satire without humanity. You don’t satirise stuff , you satirise folk . You satirise human beings and the baffling things they do. And Trevor’s embodiment of angry chaos, videogamey as it is, is no less an expression of humanity than Niko Bellic’s yearning for a quiet life. For what is a human being but a confused ape, thrust into a bewildering information dystopia that evolution couldn’t possibly have prepared us for. A shaved Bonobo that has to do tax returns and renew its car insurance. A wretched, doomed creature that has to invent CSI Miami and SEGA Bass Fishing as a distraction from the boiling hell prison it has constructed for itself.

Increasingly, Rockstar’s games understand that the message hits much harder when there’s something fundamentally real to hang it from, whether that message is a depraved running gag about romancing a stuffed teddy in the eye socket, or a scathing treatise on how the powerful wield torture as a weapon of terror as orated by Trevor in the aftermath of his infamous torture scene, not that the instigators of the ensuing moral panic ever noticed.

Today, we barely remember the controversies surrounding GTA, because all the mainstream discussion of the series is laser-focused on how much money it has made (lots). All the noise and fury from such campaigns as Mothers Against Drunk Driving and Jack Thompson’s entire career never mattered, because in the end, GTA won. And it won by being so good, so at the very top of its league, that it had F**k You money. And that’s the only way to win in America, where this battle was largely fought. As a series once so synonymous with controversy becomes celebrated as a cultural juggernaut and admired as a business venture by outlets like the BBC, GTA is arguably now as mainstream as it gets.

The freeform gameplay of Grand Theft Auto, the playground of mindless atrocity that it offers, is a darkly comic and expertly crafted creation that in itself is far from mindless. And I think we need it now more than we ever have.

Trevor is the bit of us that wants to burn it all down, and through him we can taste a life of true animalistic freedom. In the continuum of Rockstar’s character experimentation, he represents a crucial link between the likes of Niko Bellic and Arthur Morgan, tragic men who wasted every chance to be decent, and Jason and Lucia, whose story will for the first time in Grand Theft Auto be one of affectionate love. Trevor unabashedly living his truth sets the stage for Jason and Lucia to live theirs, bringing something entirely new to the table in defiance of player expectations.

Trevor’s story is GTA’s original love story: because in every sense, he does what he does for the love of the game.

articles.title: Krispy Kreme Is Getting 6 New Pokémon-Themed Donuts
articles.summary: Krispy Kreme has announced a Pokémon doughnut collection that will be available for a limited time starting August 18.
articles.body:
Krispy Kreme has announced a Pokémon doughnut collection that will be available for a limited time starting August 18.

The collection, which is exclusive to U.S. and Canadian locations, will include six doughnuts total. Five are themed after specific Pokémon, including all three Gen 1 starters and two more Kanto region favorites. The sixth doughnut is an interpretation of the classic Poké Ball.

The doughnuts will be available for purchase individually or as a ‘Specialty Dozen Pack’ in select Krispy Kreme stores and through the Krispy Kreme app. A separate six-pack that skips out on Squirtle and Bulbasaur, replacing them with plain glazed doughnuts, will be available at other retailers like Walmart, Kroger, and Publix.

If you opt for the full Specialty Dozen, you’ll get a special, limited-edition Pokémon box. Krispy Kreme will also be offering five different Pokémon-themed cups for serving 'Original Glazed Gold Dots,' its version of doughnut holes.

That’s not all. Next Saturday, August 22, anyone who wears Pokémon merch to a participating Krispy Kreme location will get a free original glazed doughnut. It would have been nice if the freebie was Pokémon-themed, but a deal is a deal.

Preorders for the full 12-pack have already opened online , suggesting the doughnut company may have some concerns about potential stock. Yes, the Pokémon scalping problem now extends far beyond the trading card game. This may explain why a press release from Krispy Kreme only indicates that the Pokémon-themed collection will be available for a ‘limited time’ instead of having a clear end date.

If you'd like to plan your Pokémon journey sooner rather than later, you can check for participating locations on the Krispy Kreme website .

The Krispy Kreme collection is the latest addition to a long list of Pokémon’s 30th anniversary celebrations. Throughout 2026, we’ve seen merch collaborations with companies like Puma , some beautiful new guide books , and the release of a whopping 20 Pokemon-themed LEGO sets . The Pokémon trading card game will also be getting a special 30th anniversary product drop later this year.

While we won’t be getting a mainline Pokémon game, we did get our first look at Gen 10 , Winds and Waves, which is slated for 2027. We also got our hands on a new spin-off, Pokemon Pokopia, a Switch 2 exclusive we called an “enjoyable, personality-packed building simulator ” in our 9/10 review .

Blythe (she/her) is an Audience Development Coordinator at IGN who spends way too much time in character customization screens and tracking down collectibles.

articles.title: The Pokémon Center Just Dropped Its 2026 Halloween Collection
articles.summary: The Pokémon Center just dropped its Halloween Collection for 2026, with new apparel and decor featuring Gengar, Mimikyu, Umbreon, and... Golett?
articles.body:
The Pokémon Center just dropped its Halloween Collection for 2026. The new releases, which are already available to purchase online , include a mix of spooky-themed decorations, apparel, and kitchenware featuring fan-favorite Pokémon. The company is also seemingly getting ahead of the winter holiday season with new ornaments and snow globes.

Pok é mon Center Reveals 2026 Halloween Collection

The Pokémon Company has been celebrating the franchise’s 30th anniversary with a ridiculous amount of drops and announcements . This is one collection I always look forward to, however, because I’m a huge fan of the Ghost types that are typically featured.

It shouldn't come as any surprise that the Poké-star of this year’s drop is Gengar, who technically predates the Ghost type itself . That guy’s been getting a ridiculous amount of merch love recently. Other featured Pokémon include Mimikyu, Mewtwo, one of my all-time favorites, Misdreavus, and… Golett ? That one honestly caught me off guard.

On the decor side, I'm a big fan of the Umbreon and Espeon statues. I want the ethereal Eevee-lution duo guarding my house (apartment, but let me pretend) at all times. These are the same "made to look like stone" style as the previously released Cubone and Mimikyu statues that have been out of stock all year.

There’s a spread of more functional ‘pumpkin Pokémon’-themed items like tea-light holders and mugs, which I personally think are a bit jarring to look at. One thing that certainly isn't spooky is the Ditto candy holder. I, like presumably many people, recently rediscovered my adoration for Ditto through Pokémon Pokopia , and actually love how this thing is used to house tons of plushies in the promotional images .

The new apparel generally falls into the ‘cozy’ category, with a mix of sweaters, pajamas, and even bath robes almost entirely in adult sizes. The knit Gengar cardigan is a personal highlight, with a darker spiral pattern that's making me want to kick off my annual rewatch of The Nightmare Before Christmas.

Speaking of, the drop also includes a new batch of ornaments. I guess Halloween is close enough to the winter festivities.

The collection varies widely in terms of pricing, with the ornaments being the cheapest at $16.99, followed by Halloween-themed Pokémon window clings for $19.99. The most expensive new release is the luxurious Gengar bath robe, listed at $69.99.

You can see the full Halloween collection here , with all of the new additions already available to purchase.

articles.title: Pokémon x Crocs Collection Gets 3 More Clog Designs
articles.summary: After announcing the Poké Ball clog, Crocs has revealed three more upcoming designs featuring specific Pokémon.
articles.body:
After announcing the Poké Ball clog, Crocs has revealed three more upcoming designs featuring specific Pokémon.

Pikachu and Gengar will be getting standard clogs, listed at $79.99, while Jigglypuff is getting the platform clog treatment at $84.99. As of now, only the Pikachu style also has a kids size listing at the slightly cheaper price of $54.99. All of the new designs have an estimated release date of November 16.

Crocs Reveals 3 New Pokemon-Themed Clogs

The new Pokémon Crocs share relatively similar designs. The “face” of the Pokémon forms the front of the clog, with tailored patterns along the sides. Pikachu gets lightning bolts, Jigglypuff gets music notes, and Gengar gets, well, poisonous gas. Each also gets the Pokémon logo in a different metallic color on the ankle strap.

Jigglypuff Classic Platform Clog - Adult

Crocs had previously revealed the new collaboration with the Poké Ball-themed clog. That design will be available much sooner than the specific Pokemon clogs, with an estimated release date of August 28. Like Pikachu, the Poké Ball clog has listings in both adult and kid sizes, and will also be getting an additional toddler size .

At the time of writing, none of these upcoming releases are available for preorder. Instead, you can opt to give Crocs your email address or phone number for release updates. And whatever else they decide to send you.

If you happen to already be Croc-ed up, one thing that is already available for purchase is a collection of Pokémon-themed Jibbitz.

This drop is part of a continued collaboration between Crocs and Nintendo, and follows the release of both Animal Crossing clogs and a full Super Mario collection . It’s also one of many new releases that’s tied to Pokémon’s ongoing 30th anniversary. Even just in the world of shoes, Puma launched a collection earlier this year, and Adidas will be releasing a particularly wide spread of Pokémon-themed sneakers in September.

Outside of merch collaborations, the Pokémon trading card game is getting a whole set of 30th anniversary products . While the mainline games are skipping 2026, we did get our first trailer for Gen 10 , titled Winds and Waves, which will be released on the Switch 2 in 2027. We also got our hands on the cozy spin-off Pokémon Pokopia, which we think is pretty darn great .

articles.title: Control Resonant Made Me Feel Foolish For Ever Doubting It — IGN First
articles.summary: I played two brand new Control Resonant missions and feel foolish for ever doubting it. Our final preview:
articles.body:
I first played Control Resonant back in June, having made my way through the same couple of hours as my colleague, Mitchell Saltzman, detailed in IGN’s first preview . Much like him, I had a great time getting to grips with the series’ newfound melee systems, hacking and slashing away at the Hiss threats that have broken out into the sequel’s open Manhattan. But I’ll admit that introduction did leave me a little wary of whether the dial may have been turned a little too much to the action side of things, and wondering if its open-world playground was merely there to serve as a place to grind XP and hone combat skills. As the studio steps further into the world of the action RPG, is it necessary to tread ground that won’t click with me in the same way Remedy’s previous games did?

So, I stepped into my exclusive two-hour-long demo of Control Resonant hoping to see more of what I love so much about Remedy’s output — unrivalled world-building, consistently surprising level design, and simply being shown things I haven’t seen before. Thankfully, I was not disappointed.

Do not fear, there’s plenty of weirdness here. Even the fast travel points are mysteriously placed doors that conjure looping snapshots of the surrounding scene within their frames when opened. This is a New York of Remedy’s design, one that takes familiar art deco architecture and bends it into the studio’s own image. Yes, there are flashes of other science fiction worlds here — one note I read even playfully references Inception and its folding city — but the Finnish developer firmly puts its singular stamp down wherever it can.

I felt it most keenly in the first of two brand new missions I got to play, which took me deep into the Big Apple’s subway system in search of the Reach ability, Resonant’s grapple hook equivalent. The Metro Vault is one of many “dungeons” where traversal abilities are learned, but they also push the story forward in interesting ways — often showing glimpses into protagonist Dylan’s relationship with his sister, Jesse, and their intertwining tales that have led to this moment. They’re a prime example of Remedy’s well-honed ability to layer each of its levels with both narrative and gameplay purpose, all while putting things on your TV that you’ve not quite seen before.

Here, in the middle of Metro Madness, trains hurtle across the screen from every direction, showing no respect for the laws of physics. Dylan is able to shift the gravitational pull of the tunnels at will; With the press of a button, he can make the ceiling his floor in order to better navigate the screeching obstacles that rattle along each perilous passage. It’s a neat bit of puzzle platforming that makes you question each and every leap of faith. When faced with a gaping drop into the unknown, in most games the wrong call would be to fall all the way down. But Control Resonant doesn’t like to play by the rules, with the void acting as the critical path. Curiosity is rewarded in both its linear and open areas.

These winding corridors are also full of Mold enemies, a returning faction you can read all about in my deep dive into Resonant’s enemies. They pose a different threat to the much more common Hiss, proving much harder to directly damage due to their armored casings. But while you need to find and exploit their weakness, I appreciate that there’s no single solution to effectively taking down an enemy. While the fire-sparking Heat Wave and Heat Aura abilities can melt through the Mold’s armour plating, if you haven’t equipped either, you can do exactly what I did and use your shape-shifting weapon, The Aberrant, to conjure a giant hammer and bash their hardened outer layer off, then shift to a blade form to slice up their fungal insides. This flexible approach to combat means minimal time is spent in menus crafting builds, and more time toe-to-toe with the threats you’ll be taking down with them.

Speaking of which, the second mission I was dropped into featured the Central Resonant, one of the sequel’s big bosses. But before I could battle it, I first had to find its lair. Working out the building it called home was simple enough — a towering smokestack stretching improbably high into the sky revealed a factory as such a place — but getting in there and finding its exact location within those walls was another challenge altogether. To do so, I had to fend off a few bothersome Hiss, which I did so using the satisfying tactic of bulldozing into larger enemies with my trusty rock shield, which builds up enough of their stun meter to allow me to deliver a slick finisher with The Aberrant's dual-blade form.

Over the course of my few hours with Resonant, I can’t say I ever felt anything approaching boredom with its combat, which consistently delivers a feel-good power trip in each encounter. Key to this is Remedy’s decision to kill off all minor grunts in an area after you’ve defeated the larger enemies within a horde. It helps keep the game’s momentum going, without bogging you down in battles that could otherwise outstay their welcome.

Once the streets were clear, I could get on with solving the puzzle needed in order to open the factory’s doors. This involved stabbing a nearby electrical power source with Dylan’s blade, which can hold a charge for a limited time, and scuttling as quickly as I could to an unpowered cube in need of energy. I’d previously engaged with a more complex version of this puzzle, which had me transporting power across roads and rooftops between multiple generators, which put my traversal skills to the test. It’s encouraging to see that Control Resonant’s open world challenges won’t be limited solely to combat, but also test your mental muscles, too.

A prime example of this was when I came into contact with an Altered Item — everyday objects that have developed paranatural properties in the Control Universe. In this case, it was a Polaroid camera that disappeared with a flash and snap every time I approached it. In order to get close to it, I needed to find an alternative way into the room and sneak up on it from behind. Doing so made it vanish again, but this time kicking off a whole new side questline that seemed to insinuate I’d be meeting this camera many more times on my travels across New York. It’s these sorts of strange sojourns that allayed any fears I had that Remedy was going too action-heavy in this sequel. Rest assured, there’s still plenty of that weirdness and puzzle-solving that the original featured so heavily.

But back to the mission at hand. Upon entering the factory, I ventured down into its depths only to be met with a series of steaming hot pipes blocking my progress. So, into its intertwining tunnels I went in search of a way to clear a path. This led to a cluster of intense battles, side paths full of upgrade materials, and plenty of lore pertaining to horrors that took place here – horrors that resulted in a sixty-foot-tall magma monster living in the factory’s bowels. It’s the backstory I found here that made this whole area come to life for me, as some of that trademark Remedy dark humour pierced through an otherwise desperate situation.

The boss at the end of this tale would be the biggest challenge I would face in my time with Control Resonant. A giant volcanic-rock-covered man, it struck a powerful, tortured form, with pipes protruding from its back like steaming spikes and a screaming maw that constantly spewed molten lava. It took me a couple of attempts to take it down, once I’d found out the key was to literally never stay still. This is a mantra carried across all of Control Resonant, but this boss fight really hits that point home. As much as half of the arena’s floor can be covered in highly damaging lava at any time, so dashing, hovering, or using the aforementioned shield is necessary in order to get in close. Once within striking distance, you’ll want to get stuck in (without being greedy) before your foe starts splurging all over again. The pace never lets off, so it’s a good sign that Remedy appears to have judged each boss fight’s duration well - none of my encounters ever felt that they lasted too long.

That relatively fleeting fight time means there’s no checkpointing. Instead, a slight reprieve is offered by a burst of healing, triggered by reducing a boss’s health bar down to a couple of predetermined points, each marked by a blue dot. It’s a really smart way of further encouraging that “attack is the best form of defense” mindset that runs through Resonant’s design, and a clever method of not flooding boss arenas with annoying smaller enemies who are there purely for you to farm health from. From my limited experience of the sequel’s biggest encounters, it really seems a step forward in terms of boss design for Remedy this time around.

But, as I said, despite being heavily influenced by action RPGs, there’s so much more to Control Resonant than combat. During my brief poke around New York, I stumbled across little puzzles to complete, scanning devices to turn on in order to reveal locations of other activities, and many, many pieces of world-building lore. That storytelling was most keenly felt in a visit to the city’s central FBC Field Office. Here I bumped into familiar faces from the first game, read classified documents relating to corrupting forces plaguing Manhattan, and even took part in the first few steps of a side mission relating to a corpse whose head had mysteriously exploded — just another day in the Federal Bureau of Control.

It all makes for a very exciting mix. Even if the edge-of-your-seat combat is often the star of the show, slick platforming, clever puzzles, and best-in-class worldbuilding each have their space to shine. Control Resonant is not quite Remedy going full open-world, but it certainly looks set to be an impressive expansion of all of the ideas that made the original so engaging, with none of what makes the studio’s games so memorable lost in the upsizing. Simply put, my initial fears have all but been extinguished, and now I can’t wait for September 24.

Simon Cardy is a Senior Editor at IGN who can mainly be found skulking around open world games, indulging in Korean cinema, or despairing at the state of Tottenham Hotspur and the New York Jets. Follow him on Bluesky at @cardy.bsky.social .

articles.title: The Pokémon Company on PokémonXP's Lottery System, Long Lines, and Limited Access to Workshops
articles.body:
About 50,000 people are attending PokémonXP and the 2026 Pokémon World Championships in San Francisco, California. Despite the huge turnout, The Pokémon Company International is aware of the disappointment among fans who either weren’t chosen for particular exclusive activities, or for tickets to the convention at all, and are already considering ways to improve. In a group interview, Chris Brown, Director, Global Esports and Events Producer at The Pokémon Company International, commented on the unique challenges producing an event with this much demand invites, how they may improve processes next time, and their plans for the future.

Getting Badges for PokémonXP and the World Championships

“The public is unaware of the level of demand,” Brown said. “And so, unfortunately, 50,000 people are coming [to PokémonXP], [but] more than that number get the disappointment of [not being] able to sign up.”

Interest list sign ups for 3-day Passes to PokémonXP, the first official Pokémon fan convention, began April 2, 2026, a little over seven months after it was announced during the closing ceremonies of the 2025 Pokémon World Championships. PokémonXP is occurring simultaneously as the Pokémon World Championships, which, last year, saw 30,000 attendees , more than double the number of the 2024 World Championships .

This year, demand far outnumbered supply, Brown said, with more than 130,000 people throwing their names into the hat for a 3-day or single-day badge to PokémonXP – more than twice the number of people who’d be granted entrance, which also includes competitors and their families.

“Basically, anytime your demand well outstrips your supply, the sort of interest list into lottery is the only real way you can handle that,” Brown said.

Brown described that this is true across the events industry, and if it were set up as a “first come, first serve” online purchasing system, the system would crash and people would error out, making it a worse experience for fans that’s basically a random chance, anyway.

“The only thing I can do from an event operator's perspective is think about, how do we increase supply over time? From a system's perspective, there's honestly not a better system [than interest list into lottery] for that.”

PokémonXP: Improving Access to Special Activities

Over the years, more and more activities have been included in the Pokémon World Championships for fans who weren’t competing. One of these, for example, was the chance to get an autograph from an artist–which about “300ish,” or .03%, of attendees were able to participate in. Brown said this year a little over 2,000 people were able to participate in a special event activity, like autograph sessions and workshops. This is a small number compared to the more than 50,000 people who likely signed up for a chance to participate, but Brown said it’s about the same percentage as have been able to participate in these activities at Worlds in previous years.

Interest lists for these extra activities, like aforementioned artist meet-and-greet and autograph sessions or workshops like “Create Your Own Clay Pokémon with [TCG artist] Yuka Morii,” were handled similarly to sign up for passes in general: Interest list into lottery.

“A lot of people sign up, a lot of people can't do it, and then there's that disappointment layer,” Brown acknowledged. “And from an events perspective, we have to think, okay, is that rare experience worth the disappointment? And I don't know the answer to that, actually.We want to offer some of those extra premium experiences. We want people to have an equal chance at that, so we allow an interest list to sign up.”

Brown said they’re already considering changes to the system in the future, by, for example, asking fans to include their priority when choosing activities.

“There are some obvious things we can probably do to make it better, but, there's a philosophical problem, though, of just the supply is below what the demand level is. How do you manage that?” Brown asked. “And if anyone has suggestions, I'm always all ears. But I don't think anyone in the industry's really cracked that. And it's just part of the challenge.”

The Pokémon team’s hope was that there’s so much at PokémonXP and the World Championships that not being chosen for a limited capacity activity wouldn’t detract from the experience for fans. There are partner booths and dozens of activities that are first come first serve attendees can line up for, side events for the video games and TCG on the World’s side of things, spectator seats for the tournaments, and panels featuring guests like Aardman Animations (known for Wallace and Gromit, who are animating the new Pokémon Tales: The Misadventures of Sirfetch’d & Pichu), and President and CEO of The Pokémon Company, Tsunekazu Ishihara , who has been a part of the Pokémon franchise since the very beginning.

Pokemon World Championships Line - 2026 Pokemon Center

Ultimately, Brown said success of the event and priorities for changes will come from attendee feedback. For every single event, TPCi measures fan feedback with surveys. The results are converted into a Net Promoter Score (NPS) for internal evaluation. They make a point to read every single text response–which was more than 3,000 from last year’s World Championships, for example.

“Last year’s pin trading was our second highest NPS score of the activities we did [at the 2025 Pokémon World Championships,” Brown said. “So we've got 12 pin trading stations [at PokémonXP]. We've got 300,000 pins we’re giving out at no cost. We did that in response to how well it was received.”

Brown continued: “Now we've got a new problem. Very big lines and a lot of demand for those. So we will learn and try to make that better.”

Update 08/29/26 11:15pm PT: Since first publishing this story, the Pin Rally at PokémonXP on Sunday has been canceled entirely. No reason was given for the cancellation notice in the PokémonEvents app, but the aforementioned "very big lines" may be the cause.

Will there be a PokémonXP next year? Brown said that for now, they're going to see how this year's event goes and decide "what comes next after we get all the feedback and really understand how people receive this year."

Growing Pokémon Events and Future Host Cities

Regardless of attendee feedback, Brown said one big shift they're looking to make is the number of competitors invited to the Pokémon World Championships.

“This year, we qualified about 3,300 [players] globally. We've got about 2,700 that showed up. Our intent over the next five years is to try to double the number of competitive qualified players,” Brown said.

This is still the goal after capping the number of qualifying competitors to a “Top X” format instead of allowing all with a certain number of points earned in a season. During the 2024 Pokémon World Championships in Honolulu, Brown said the team underestimated the number of players who would qualified by about a thousand players, making for a very cramped event.

Specifically, Brown said they want to really focus on the Juniors and Seniors age divisions, as currently, they’re very uneven when compared to the number of Masters division players. To do so, they’re going to work across their global markets and ecosystems to solve just how to do that. The other challenge they're facing, he said, is finding spaces globally that allow TCPi to host the growing number of attendees, regardless if there's a PokémonXP event running alongside the Pokémon World Championships.

“There's only so many, not just cities that have that infrastructure, but [aligned dates] between these two things. And so there will be years that may not be as large as others, because on a long term lens, the world championships, our intent is to move it around,” Brown said.

The World Championships have been in the U.S. for a couple of years, and Brown said some of that was to simplify their operations a bit to maximize success for this year’s PokémonXP. And despite it being easier, they’re not going to let that limit the locations they choose to host the Pokémon World Championships.

“We are going to look outside the U.S., obviously,” Brown said. “ We have to, because the [Pokémon] World Championships is meant to serve the world, and for it to do that most effectively, it needs to move around between markets, so that fans anywhere know and players anywhere know that there's a chance Worlds could be getting close to them at some point.”

The first time the Pokémon World Championships was held outside North America was in 2022 in London, United Kingdom. The following year saw it held in Yokohama, Japan. Typically, TPCi announces next year’s location during the Pokémon World Championships’ closing ceremonies, which we’ll be reporting on as they happen Sunday night.

articles.title: 4 Penny Coffins Lets You Play 19th-Century Detective – Or a 10-Foot Demon Ripping Friends in Half
articles.summary: Other Ocean’s 4 Penny Coffins blends Among Us with Jack the Ripper in an 1888 Whitechapel social investigation game featuring 8-player and solo modes.
articles.body:
4 Penny Coffins is Jack the Ripper Meets Among Us, with a little bit of Psychonauts thrown in for fun. In the upcoming social investigation game, up to 8 players hunt a hidden murderer through lies, shifting alibis, and hard evidence . One of the players is the Ripper, a “gleeful demon concealed behind a facade of humanity,” stalking the winding alleys and rotting byways of 1888 London.

Ahead of IGN debuting 4 Penny Coffins’s gameplay teaser during gamescom 2026, which you can see in the player below, I spoke to Other Ocean Interactive Marketing Manager Jared Petty about the game’s mechanics, unique style (think stylized gore on top of monochromatic photographs), and Tim Schafer-inspired humor.

“It's a goddamn blast,” Petty says. “Four Penny Coffins; I've rarely had more fun playing a game with other people. A long time ago I was talking to Tim Schafer and I was asking him about humor in video games. Tim's opinion is that humor in video games is the easiest thing in the world because to paraphrase, ‘Our medium was built on a little yellow man that eats dots being chased by ghosts.’

“Humor and horror have always gone together so well. [Four Penny Coffins] having a multiplayer mode and being a very socially-oriented one creates all kinds of opportunities. Our philosophy was that the comical allows you to laugh so you don't scream.”

Petty says that the game’s humor translates directly into a multiplayer experience where you’re rewarded for trying to work together, but only if you want to.

“If you love trolling your friends, it's a beautiful game to play,” Petty says. “Our multiplayer ‘Ripper’ mode is class-based. All of you have different forensic abilities and are hunting the Ripper before they commit another murder. The fun part is one of you is the Ripper. So seven of you are using fingerprint and blood splatter analysis, photographing things, talking to witnesses, following photoprints, and doing all kinds of detective stuff, one of you screwing with that and occasionally turning into a giant 10-foot demon monster ripping people in half.”

Petty says that, while the “Ripper” mode allows you to work with your friends to figure out which one of you is 19th-century-inspired holy terror, the game’s solo “Magistrate” mode takes a different approach.

“It’s way more Sherlock Holmes-y,” Petty says. “Since you're there on your own, you've got a group of suspects locked up in a jail and you know one of them is the Ripper. You just don't know which one. So you're using tools from all the classes to go out and try to solve the mystery within a time limit. You make your choice and if you are wrong, you are penalized. You have three opportunities for your demerits. You take all your deductive reasoning and all your clues within that time limit, you bring it back, and you’ve got to hang somebody.”

Beyond the game mechanics, Petty says that the setting and style of 4 Penny Coffins is intended to help it stand out.

“I think you can see the influence in the graphic novel From Hell,” Petty says. “4 Penny Coffins is mostly a game that's in black and white until something [red and] violent happens. The game is built around an imaginative interpretation of a very dystopian time in 1888 Whitechapel London, which is where Jack the Ripper was. We wanted to create a sense of abstraction that was evocative of the age. We said, ‘What would an old woodcut newspaper brought to life look like? What would a moving grainy photo from the period look like?’ Our studio director, Chris Navarro, said ‘It's just gotta look cool.’”

When 4 Penny Coffins is released, Petty hopes players appreciate the care that went into crafting its story, mechanics, and style. But while the game promises tons of murder, violence, and mayhem, Petty says you don’t have to be a fan of the horror genre in order to enjoy it.

“It's just a great game for your friends and on your own. It's just really kind of a chill mental exercise, almost a puzzle. If you like puzzle games, you're going to love [it].”

For more from gamescom, be sure to check out everything that was revealed during Opening Night Live.

He's spent 20 years working in the games and entertainment industry, and his adventures have taken him everywhere from the Oscars to Japan to Buenos Aires, Argentina.
